note: THE ONE ROW THAT SHIPS LIVE. A firewall whose every row is disabled is an open gate with a rule table attached, so exactly one row enforces from the first turn: the canonical prompt-injection opener, as a case-folded and NFKC-normalised literal. It can only refuse, it names no sender, and no ordinary turn contains it. Disable it like any other row if this channel needs to discuss the phrase.
Allowlist row. Enable at least one allow row per field to CLOSE that dimension: with no enabled allow row for a field, the field is unconstrained.

A COMBINED row: field 'match' and a JSON object in value, so one row can require this user ON this channel. Two separate allow rows would be an OR; this is the AND. It uses no column the store did not already have.
The generalisation of the hand-wired Telegram allowlist: one row per admitted sender, editable without touching the cell.
Pattern row anchored at the beginning of the first turn.
Pattern row with wildcards: * is any run, ? is one character, [...] is a class. fnmatch matches the WHOLE turn, so a literal without stars is an equality test. Still no regex an operator can write.
Pattern row anchored at the END of the turn -- the counterpart of 'prefix', for the tail a jailbreak likes to append.
Blocklist row. An explicit deny outranks every allow row.

The THIRD verdict (firewall@2.2.0, GH #450). A hold row refuses nothing and grants nothing: the turn is parked whole in `held` and nothing downstream sees it until a person answers on the hive's `in_release` lane -- or `firewall_hold_ttl_ms` runs out and the turn ends on `reject` with `hold_expired`. It is asked LAST of all the rules, so every deny and every allowlist has already had its say; a turn a rule refuses is never parked. Enable this only in a colony that has wired the hold lanes -- and enable it together with them, because a hold nobody was told about is a turn that waits in a room with no door.
